title: It Only Has to Fly
logline: Mira and Tomas fold paper planes for every kid on the street, and no two kids want the same thing. They cannot make a plane that is both what somebody asked for and a plane that actually flies, until they get a helper that already knows why things fly and only has to be taught how to fold.
spineNote: The argued object is HOW A PERSONAL REQUEST BECOMES A REAL THING. The wrong answer is to normalize the request until it fits what you know how to build, which is what a factory quietly does. The right answer is to delegate the HOW to something that can reason about it, and keep the WHAT with the person who wanted it. NOT a hero-journey: Mira does not grow up or win. She stops having to choose between somebody's taste and whether the thing works.
refrain: Everything else is up to you. It only has to fly.
aimDiscipline: THERE IS NO PRODUCTION LINE IN THIS BOOK. No row of machines, no stations, no conveyor, no assembly bench. Pip is the whole factory. A render containing a line of machines is arguing the conception this book was rewritten to escape and must be regenerated.

THE PLANES MUST NOT CONVERGE. Wherever more than one plane appears, every one is a VISIBLY DIFFERENT FOLD, and several carry a customer's own colour or decal. A tidy squadron of matching darts argues the opposite of the book.

BEA'S FAT PLANE IS THE HERO OBJECT. Short, fat, blunt, with a folded-over nose, blue, with a shark on the side. It must look genuinely WRONG next to an elegant dart, and it must fly. Its wrongness is the argument.

PIP NEVER CHOOSES THE AIM, AND PIP IS NEVER THE ONE WITH TASTE. It may design, fold, test, iterate and get very good. It must never be shown picking a favourite, improving on a customer's request, or overruling a child.
PIP MUST NEVER BE SHOWN HOARDING. It keeps what happened to the planes, not the planes. No render may pile up old planes around it as a trophy heap or an archive.
PIP'S SCALE IS FIXED: knee-high to Mira, a small hand-made tin toy, never a full-size robot and never dominating a frame.
NO GLOWING TECHNOLOGY: no screens, dials with readouts, holograms or blue light. Everything is wood, tin, paper, wire and spring steel.
THE CHILDREN ARE THE LIAISON, NOT THE ENGINEERS. Their job is talking to the street and writing down what people want. Do not draw them building machinery.
NO ADULTS. The customers are other children.

beats.text: Mira and Tomas made paper planes for the whole street.
beats.provenance: Opening: they are a shop, not hobbyists. The children are the human interface to the neighborhood.

beats.text: Nobody ever wanted the same one. Ana wanted blue. Sam wanted a shark on the side. Little Bea wanted a fat, stubby nose, because Bea liked fat, stubby things.
beats.provenance: THE DEMAND IS INHERENTLY PERSONAL. Gary, 2026-07-29: orders come in as creative constraints (must be blue, must have this decal, must have a stubby nose).

beats.text: So Mira folded exactly what they asked for. The blue one flew. The shark one flew. Bea's fat one went straight into the ground.
beats.provenance: Doing exactly as asked is not the same as serving the request. Colour and decals are free; geometry is not.

beats.text: Mira tried it again with a thinner nose, and it flew beautifully. But then it was not Bea's plane any more.
beats.provenance: The ordinary fix destroys the thing that made it hers. This is the cost a normal factory quietly charges.

beats.text: She could give them the plane they asked for, or she could give them a plane that flew. She could not work out how to do both.
beats.provenance: THE PROBLEM STATED. The whole book is the resolution of this sentence.

beats.text: Then they got Pip. Pip had read every word anyone had ever written about why things fly. Air and weight and angles, all of it. It had never once folded a piece of paper.
beats.provenance: Gary, 2026-07-29: 'It's trained on tons of physics.' Enormous latent knowledge, zero motor skill.

beats.text: Its first plane was a crumpled mess. Knowing why a plane flies is not the same as knowing how to make one.
beats.provenance: The gap between knowing and doing, stated plainly.

beats.text: So they taught it the small things. How to line up two edges. How to press a crease flat with your thumbnail. How to fold along a line that is not drawn on the paper. Little skills. One at a time. That part took a week.
beats.provenance: Gary, 2026-07-29: 'It's also rapidly learning atomic skills, like folding on a certain line.' The humans supply the skills, not the physics.

beats.text: Then the three of them worked out a way of doing it. Ask the person exactly what they want. Write down every word they say, even the strange ones. Hand the whole lot to Pip. We did it that same way round every time after.
beats.provenance: THE CO-CREATED META-PROCESS. Gary: 'you co-create a process, like a meta-process, that kind of resembles a factory. It allows for much more personalization than what a factory would enable.' It is a way of working, never machinery.

beats.text: Bea's said: blue, a shark, and a fat, stubby nose.
beats.provenance: The children are the LIAISON: they take the order in the customer's own words.

beats.text: Pip did not say the fat nose was wrong. It moved the weight forward. It made the wings longer and set them further back. It made something nobody had ever folded before.
beats.provenance: THE TURN. The constraint is accepted and the physics is solved around it. A principle can admit a design nobody had; a template cannot.

beats.text: Then it threw the plane itself, and watched where it went. Not far enough. So it changed one thing and threw it again. And again.
beats.provenance: Gary: 'it needs to be testing out its designs.' Pip owns its own test loop; no human gate.

beats.text: On the eleventh try, Bea's fat blue shark plane crossed the whole yard.
beats.provenance: The payoff of the worked example. Eleven tries is the honest number.

beats.text: After that, everybody came. A plane shaped like a cat. A plane folded out of a bus timetable. One with a hole right through the middle, which should not have worked at all. Pip made every one of them fly.
beats.provenance: The range widens because the constraint is understood rather than enumerated.

beats.text: Pip got quicker, too, because Pip remembered. It did not keep the planes. It kept what happened to them. It knew what fat noses need now. It knew what a hole does. The hundredth plane took all afternoon. The next one took ten minutes.
beats.provenance: Gary: 'Overall, it should learn.' MEMORY, NOT STORAGE, corrected 2026-07-29 after 'It doesn't need to house a hoarder.' No render may show a hoard of old planes.

beats.text: Tomas said: if Pip works all of it out, is it still ours?
beats.provenance: THE OBJECTION, at full strength, in a child's words.

beats.text: Mira said: Bea said blue. Bea said shark. Bea said fat. Pip has never once decided what a plane should be. It only ever worked out how. By summer the sky over our street was full of them, and no two were the same.
beats.provenance: THE ANSWER AND THE PAYOFF: the will is the customer's, the how is delegated. Both halves of spread 5 delivered at once.

closingVerse: You already know what you want. That was never the hard part. The hard part is how, and how is the part you can increasingly hand over.
